title: Steel and Scrap
subtitle: What the Armor Leaves Behind · Chapter 6 of 40
content:
The Brotherhood did not arrive the next day.

Or the day after that.

A working transmitter did not mean a vertibird would materialize the moment Danse wanted one. The station remained what it had been: three exhausted soldiers, one persistent outsider, and a building held together by scavenged wire, habit, and stubbornness.

I stayed.

At first I told myself it was because Cambridge had walls.

Then because Haylen needed help repairing the signal amplifier.

Then because the workbench was better than mine.

By the time I ran out of practical excuses, Danse had started setting aside coffee for me.

It was terrible coffee.

That did not seem to matter.

“You boil it too long,” I told him one morning.

He stood at the small hot plate in the back room, watching a dented pot with tactical suspicion.

“It’s coffee.”

“That is not a defense.”

“It contains caffeine.”

“So does a lot of medicine. I don’t want that in a mug either.”

He poured two cups.

“You complain every time.”

“And yet you keep giving it to me.”

“You keep drinking it.”

We looked at each other.

He had me there.

I took the cup.

“Thank you.”

“You’re welcome.”

The exchange should not have felt domestic.

The station itself prevented that. Rhys was cleaning a rifle at the front desk while muttering about perimeter discipline. Haylen had fallen asleep over a terminal with one cheek pressed against her sleeve. A generator coughed outside. Somewhere in the walls, a radroach scratched with criminal confidence.

Still, standing across from Danse in the yellow morning light, drinking terrible coffee he had made without being asked, I felt something settle.

He noticed me looking toward Haylen.

“She was up most of the night.”

“So were you.”

“I slept.”

“When?”

“Enough.”

“That is not a time.”

His eyes narrowed.

“You keep unusually detailed track of my sleep schedule.”

“You make it easy by barely having one.”

He took a drink.

His face did not react to the coffee at all.

That might have been the most disturbing thing about him.

After breakfast, he put me through firearms drills.

I had not agreed to firearms drills.

Apparently remaining within fifteen feet of Paladin Danse for multiple consecutive days constituted implied consent to training.

“Again,” he said.

I lowered Righteous Authority.

“I hit all six targets.”

“Your grouping is inconsistent.”

“They are cans.”

“Today they’re cans. Tomorrow they could be synths.”

“Do synths often stand in neat rows on fence posts?”

“Again.”

I muttered something rude.

“What was that?”

“I said ‘outstanding.’”

“Your sarcasm needs work.”

I fired again.

The last can jumped from the fence.

Danse inspected the grouping.

“Better.”

I stared at him until he added, “Much better.”

“See? Growth.”

“In you, perhaps.”

“Hopeless.”

His eyes warmed.

Then a noise came from the street.

The change in him was instant.

Danse moved between me and the doorway before either of us knew what the sound was. His hand went to his sidearm. His body blocked mine on pure reflex.

A brahmin wandered past the entrance wearing half a shopping cart as luggage.

Silence.

I looked at Danse’s back.

He slowly lowered his weapon.

“That,” I said, “was terrifying.”

“The animal could have been accompanied.”

“By what? An organized raider dairy operation?”

He stepped aside.

“You mock caution until the day caution saves your life.”

“I’m not mocking caution.”

“You’re laughing.”

“I’m mocking you.”

“That’s becoming a pattern.”

“Yes.”

He seemed about to say something else when his attention shifted past me.

Rhys stood in the doorway.

“Paladin. Patrol?”

Danse’s expression hardened back into command.

“Five minutes.”

Rhys nodded and disappeared.

The warmth vanished with him.

Not because Danse was pretending around me.

Because command was another suit of armor, and he wore it whenever someone under him was watching.

I understood that more each day.

The patrol took us through Cambridge toward an old medical building. Haylen had marked it as a possible source of antiseptics and circuitry. Rhys came with us, limping less than before and resenting me more efficiently.

Inside, we found raiders.

The fight was ugly and close.

At one point Rhys pushed through a doorway before Danse cleared the second angle. A shotgun blast caught him across the shoulder plate and spun him sideways.

Danse’s response was immediate.

He put two laser shots through the shooter, dragged Rhys behind cover, and turned on him.

“What the hell were you thinking?”

“I had the room.”

“You had half the room.”

“I saw—”

“You saw what was in front of you. That’s not the same thing.”

Rhys’s face tightened.

“Yes, sir.”

Danse checked the wound himself.

His hands were careful despite the anger.

Afterward, on the walk back, he barely spoke.

Rhys went ahead.

I stayed beside Danse.

“You saved him.”

“He shouldn’t have needed saving.”

“People make mistakes.”

“Not all mistakes are survivable.”

The words came too quickly.

I looked at him.

He was staring at Rhys’s back.

“Is this about the four names?”

His jaw tightened.

“Yes.”

The admission surprised both of us.

We walked several steps in silence.

“I read them,” I said. “Brach. Worwick. Dawes. Keane.”

Danse stopped.

The street around us was empty except for weeds moving in the wind.

I expected him to be angry.

Instead he looked tired.

“Keane died here,” he said. “Right outside the station. The others…”

He trailed off.

“You don’t have to tell me.”

“I know.”

That mattered.

He looked toward the station in the distance.

“Maybe I should.”

Not now, his face said.

But someday.

I nodded.

We started walking again.

As we reached the barricade, Danse held the door for me.

An absurdly ordinary gesture.

I passed him and said, “Thanks.”

“Don’t make anything of it.”

“I wasn’t.”

“You were smiling.”

“I smile sometimes.”

“I’ve noticed.”

He said it without thinking.

Then his expression changed.

So did mine.

Rhys called from inside before either of us could decide what to do with the sentence.

Danse cleared his throat.

“After you.”

I walked into the station.

Behind me, the door shut with a heavy steel click.

The sound felt suspiciously like a line being crossed.

Living at the station—because apparently that was what I was doing now—taught me the shape of Danse’s days.

He woke before everyone else.

I discovered this because I woke early once to the soft clink of free weights in what had once been an evidence room. Danse was inside in a sleeveless undershirt, counting repetitions under his breath with the grim focus of a man personally offended by fatigue.

I leaned against the doorway.

“Do you ever do anything casually?”

He lowered the bar.

“You’re awake.”

“Sharp observation.”

“It’s 0500.”

“That explains why I hate the world.”

He sat up and reached for a towel.

“Physical readiness is part of my duty.”

“You could be physically ready at seven.”

“No.”

“Six-thirty?”

“No.”

“Compromise means both people suffer.”

“That is not what compromise means.”

I stepped into the room and examined the collection of scavenged weights. Several were old engine parts threaded onto a steel pipe.

“You made these.”

“Rhys did.”

That surprised me enough that I looked toward the sleeping area.

Danse noticed.

“He is more resourceful than his disposition suggests.”

“That is the kindest insult I’ve ever heard.”

“It was not an insult.”

“Of course not.”

He gave me the look I was beginning to collect.

A few minutes later he showed me how to brace the improvised bar so it would not roll off its stand. Then he corrected my grip. Then my stance. Then, because he was Danse, he turned the entire interaction into a safety briefing.

“You are taking this very seriously.”

“Injury is preventable.”

“So is boredom.”

“Your priorities concern me.”

But he was smiling when he said it.

Afterward we sat on the floor sharing a bottle of purified water.

The station was still quiet. Haylen’s transmitter clicked softly in the next room. Rhys snored with an aggression that seemed personally directed at sleep.

Danse leaned his head back against the wall.

For once, no helmet. No rifle in his hands. No one asking him for a decision.

“You look tired,” I said.

“I’m fine.”

“Your favorite lie.”

His eyes opened.

“I don’t lie.”

“You reorganized three ammunition crates at midnight.”

“That needed to be done.”

“They were already organized.”

“Poorly.”

I let the silence sit.

Eventually he looked away.

“Sleep has been difficult since the expedition.”

The expedition.

Not yet the names. Not yet the details.

But it was something.

I passed him the water.

“You don’t have to tell me.”

“I know.”

That seemed to surprise him too.

Most people, given a crack in armor, tried to pry it wider.

I knew enough about damaged things to leave pressure off a fracture until it was ready to bear weight.

Danse took another drink.

“Thank you.”

“For what?”

“Not asking.”

I shrugged.

“When you want me to know, you’ll tell me.”

His eyes met mine.

Something in the room changed—not romance, not yet. Something quieter and more important.

Trust did not always arrive as a confession.

Sometimes it arrived as the decision that one would be safe when it came.
